concepts.name: RBI's Establishment, Legal Status, and Ownership Structure
key_dimensions: Founded via RBI Act 1934, commenced operations April 1, 1935 — private ownership initially, nationalized in 1949
Fully owned by Government of India vs. Federal Reserve (USA) ownership model — common confusion trap
Distinction between RBI as a 'statutory body' vs. 'constitutional body' vs. 'department of government'
Headquarters: Kolkata initially, shifted to Mumbai (then Bombay) in 1937 — factual trap

concepts.name: RBI's Monetary Policy Mandate and Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) Framework
key_dimensions: Amendment of RBI Act Section 45ZA in 2016 — formal legal basis for inflation targeting
Current CPI inflation target: 4% with ±2% band (2–6%) — 'headline CPI' not WPI or core inflation
Failure to maintain target for 3 consecutive quarters triggers RBI's obligation to report to government
Distinction between FIT framework (post-2016) and earlier multiple indicator approach — evolution trap
RBI's primary objective: price stability 'while keeping in mind the objective of growth' — hierarchy matters

concepts.name: Monetary Policy Committee (MPC): Composition, Powers, and Limitations
key_dimensions: 6 members: 3 from RBI (Governor as Chairperson, Deputy Governor, one RBI officer) + 3 external members appointed by GoI
MPC decides only the policy repo rate — not CRR, SLR, or other instruments (RBI retains those)
Voting: majority wins; Governor has casting vote in case of tie — asymmetric power design
External members: 4-year term, not eligible for reappointment — independence mechanism
MPC vs. Technical Advisory Committee on Monetary Policy (TACMP) — predecessor body confusion

concepts.name: Policy Rate Corridor: Repo, Reverse Repo, MSF, and SDF
key_dimensions: Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) corridor: SDF (floor) — Repo (policy rate) — MSF (ceiling)
Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) introduced April 2022 replacing fixed-rate reverse repo as the floor — key recent change
SDF vs. Reverse Repo: SDF is uncollateralized (no securities given to banks) — structural difference
Marginal Standing Facility (MSF): banks can borrow above SLR limit (up to 1% of NDTL) at MSF rate
Width of corridor determines volatility of overnight money market rates — monetary transmission link

concepts.name: Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR): Mechanics, Scope, and Exemptions
key_dimensions: Maintained as a percentage of Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) — 'net' is a trap word
CRR balances held with RBI earn NO interest — critical distinction from SLR securities
RBI Act Section 42: no statutory floor or ceiling for CRR since 2006 amendment — RBI has full discretion
Entities required to maintain CRR: scheduled commercial banks; non-scheduled banks under different provisions
CRR as a tool of liquidity absorption vs. rate-based tools — transmission mechanism difference

concepts.name: Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR): Eligible Assets, Limits, and FALLCR
key_dimensions: SLR maintained in gold, cash, or approved securities (predominantly government securities) — 'approved' is precise
Banking Regulation Act Section 24: statutory basis; current SLR is 18% — ceiling is 40%, floor removed
SLR vs. CRR: SLR earns returns (G-Sec yields); CRR earns nothing — a frequent comparison trap
FALLCR (Facility to Avail Liquidity for Liquidity Coverage Ratio): portion of SLR usable for LCR — Basel III link
HTM (Held to Maturity) classification of SLR securities and its implications for mark-to-market losses

concepts.name: RBI's Role as Banker to Government and Debt Manager
key_dimensions: RBI manages Centre's public debt under RBI Act; state governments' debt by agreement — Centre vs. State asymmetry
Ways and Means Advances (WMA): short-term credit facility to government — not 'printing money' directly
Separation of debt management from monetary policy: proposed PDMA (Public Debt Management Agency) — pending reform and conflict-of-interest argument
RBI's role in government securities market: primary dealer system, OMOs, and yield management
Overdraft facility to states: rules tightened post-2019 — fiscal discipline mechanism

concepts.name: Open Market Operations (OMOs) and Quantitative Easing Distinction
key_dimensions: OMO purchase (RBI buys G-Secs): injects liquidity; OMO sale: absorbs liquidity — direction confusion trap
Operation Twist: simultaneous purchase of long-term and sale of short-term securities to flatten yield curve
OMO vs. QE: OMO is a standard liquidity tool; QE involves large-scale unconventional asset purchases — India vs. advanced economy context
Government Securities Acquisition Programme (GSAP) introduced in 2021 — India's near-QE measure during COVID
OMO's impact on yield curve vs. policy rate's impact — transmission channel distinction

concepts.name: RBI as Lender of Last Resort (LOLR) and Emergency Liquidity Mechanisms
key_dimensions: Classic Bagehot principle: lend freely, at penalty rate, against good collateral — RBI's adaptation
LOLR applies to solvent but illiquid banks — solvency vs. liquidity distinction is a trap
Emergency Credit Line vs. routine LAF operations — graduated liquidity support framework
Distinction: LOLR function (RBI) vs. deposit insurance function (DICGC) — two separate safety net layers
Recent application: Yes Bank reconstruction 2020 — RBI's LOLR and resolution powers invoked together

concepts.name: Banking Regulation and Supervisory Powers of RBI
key_dimensions: Legal basis: Banking Regulation Act 1949 for commercial banks; RBI Act 1934 for NBFCs and RBI itself
RBI supervises: commercial banks, urban cooperative banks (post-2020 amendment), NBFCs — but NOT insurance companies (IRDAI) or securities firms (SEBI)
Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework: triggers (capital, NPA, leverage), restrictions imposed — not a 'resolution' mechanism
Differentiated banking licenses: payments banks, small finance banks — RBI's licensing power and conditions
RBI vs. NHB vs. NABARD vs. SIDBI: RBI's supervisory relationship with these apex refinancing institutions

concepts.name: Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs): Regulation, Classification, and Scale-Based Framework
key_dimensions: Definition: company doing financial business but NOT accepting demand deposits and NOT part of payment-settlement system
Scale-Based Regulation (SBR) framework (2021): Base Layer, Middle Layer, Upper Layer, Top Layer — replaces activity-based framework
NBFCs vs. Banks: NBFCs cannot issue cheques, not covered by DICGC (deposit insurance) — key distinctions
Systemically Important NBFCs (NBFC-SI): asset size threshold ₹500 crore — differential regulatory intensity
Shadow banking risk: interconnectedness of NBFCs with banks — IL&FS crisis as case study for regulatory gaps

concepts.name: Priority Sector Lending (PSL): Targets, Categories, and PSLC Mechanism
key_dimensions: Overall PSL target: 40% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) — 'adjusted' not gross credit
Sub-targets: Agriculture 18% (with 10% for small/marginal farmers), Weaker Sections 12%, Micro Enterprises 7.5%
Foreign banks (20+ branches) vs. smaller foreign banks — differential PSL targets (40% vs. 40% with different sub-targets)
Priority Sector Lending Certificates (PSLCs): tradeable certificates allowing banks to buy/sell PSL compliance — market mechanism
RIDF (Rural Infrastructure Development Fund) contribution when PSL targets are missed — penalty-like mechanism via NABARD

concepts.name: Capital Adequacy Framework: Basel Norms and India's Implementation
key_dimensions: Basel III capital requirements: Tier 1 (going-concern capital: CET1 + AT1) and Tier 2 (gone-concern) — hierarchy matters
India's minimum CRAR: 9% (higher than Basel III's 8%) — India's conservative stance
Capital Conservation Buffer (CCB): 2.5% of RWA — must be met with CET1; restricts dividends if breached
Counter-Cyclical Capital Buffer (CCyB): 0–2.5%, activated by RBI — currently at 0% in India
AT1 bonds (Additional Tier 1): perpetual, discretionary coupon, can be written down — Yes Bank AT1 write-down controversy

concepts.name: Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) Framework for Banks
key_dimensions: Three trigger indicators: Capital (CRAR/CET1), Asset Quality (Net NPA ratio), Profitability (Return on Assets) — leverage removed in 2021 revision
PCA is a supervisory tool, NOT a resolution mechanism — banks under PCA can continue operations with restrictions
Restrictions under PCA: dividend distribution, branch expansion, lending restrictions (risk-weighted asset growth) — graduated
PCA for NBFCs: extended to large NBFCs in 2022 — expansion of framework beyond banks
Exit from PCA: requires sustained improvement across all parameters for at least 4 quarters

concepts.name: Deposit Insurance: DICGC Coverage, Scope, and Recent Reforms
key_dimensions: Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC): subsidiary of RBI — ownership matters
Insurance coverage: ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank (increased from ₹1 lakh in 2020) — 'per bank' not per branch
Covered entities: commercial banks, cooperative banks, RRBs, LABs, small finance banks — NOT NBFCs, NOT payment banks (no insured deposits)
DICGC (Amendment) Act 2021: 90-day timeline for paying insured deposits even during moratorium — depositor protection reform
Premium paid by banks (not depositors): 12 paise per ₹100 of assessable deposits annually

concepts.name: RBI's Foreign Exchange Management Role and External Sector Interventions
key_dimensions: FEMA 1999 (not FERA) is the operative law; RBI is the primary regulator for forex transactions
Current Account transactions: fully convertible; Capital Account: partially convertible — India's exchange rate regime
RBI's forex reserve management: objectives hierarchy — safety, liquidity, returns (in that order)
Forex intervention: RBI intervenes to reduce volatility, not to target a specific exchange rate level — official policy stance
Swap windows, forward market interventions, NDF market — tools beyond spot market intervention

concepts.name: RBI's Governance: Central Board, Governor's Powers, and Section 7 Controversy
key_dimensions: Central Board: Governor + 4 Deputy Governors + 10 GoI-nominated directors + 4 directors from local boards — composition trap
Governor appointed by GoI (not RBI Board) — appointment process and term (currently 3 years, renewable)
Section 7 of RBI Act: GoI can issue directions to RBI in public interest after consultation — never formally invoked before 2018 controversy
RBI's functional autonomy vs. formal subordination to GoI — constitutional and legal status of independence
Central Board's role: oversight, not monetary policy (MPC does that) — clear demarcation

concepts.name: RBI's Economic Capital Framework (ECF) and Surplus Transfer to Government
key_dimensions: Bimal Jalan Committee (2019) recommendations: defined 'Realized Equity' and 'Revaluation Balances' — two-component framework
Contingency Risk Buffer (CRB): target range 5.5–6.5% of RBI's balance sheet — below this triggers retention of surplus
RBI transfers surplus (profit) to GoI: fiscal implications — 'dividend' misnomer, technically 'surplus transfer'
Currency and Gold Revaluation Account (CGRA): unrealized gains, NOT available for distribution — critical distinction
Controversy: whether RBI is 'over-capitalized' — government's claim vs. RBI's risk-based capital needs argument

concepts.name: Payment and Settlement Systems: RBI's Regulatory Role and Key Mechanisms
key_dimensions: Payment and Settlement Systems Act 2007: legal basis for RBI's regulation of payment systems
RBI operates RTGS (Real Time Gross Settlement) and NEFT; UPI operated by NPCI (not directly by RBI) — ownership distinction
NPCI: not-for-profit entity promoted by RBI and banks — RBI's indirect control vs. direct control
Prepaid Payment Instruments (PPIs), Payment Aggregators, Payment Gateways — RBI regulates differently
Systemically Important Payment Systems (SIPS): RTGS and CCIL designated — failure could trigger systemic risk

concepts.name: Monetary Transmission Mechanism: Channels, Lags, and MCLR/EBLR Framework
key_dimensions: Transmission channels: interest rate channel, credit channel, exchange rate channel, asset price channel — multiple pathways
Base Rate → MCLR (2016) → External Benchmark Lending Rate/EBLR (2019) — evolution driven by transmission failure
EBLR: retail and MSME loans mandatorily linked to external benchmarks (repo rate, T-bill, FBIL rate) — not MCLR
Transmission asymmetry: rate cuts transmit slower than rate hikes — structural stickiness issue
Liquidity conditions as prerequisite for rate transmission — 'last mile' problem in monetary policy
